 ORDER
This petition has a checkered history.

The petitioner is knocking at the doors of this Court for the second time questioning the land acquisition proceeding initiated by the third respondent-State under the provisions of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board Act, 1966 (hereinafter referred to as ' the Act' for short).
2.

sentences.text: The petitioner is a Company, that purchased the land in the year 1966 which measured 11 acres in Sy. No.37/2 of Kapanur Village, Taluk and District Kalaburagi.
The State initiated the acquisition proceeding by issuing notice under NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 Section 28(1) of the Act.
The petitioner contends that mandatory procedures contemplated under Section 28 of the Act are not followed.
The petitioner was not heard, notice is not issued after passing the award, the compensation is not paid, and the acquisition proceeding has lapsed.

3. On these premises, the petitioner approached the KIADB in 2009 with a request to set aside Section 28(1) notification and to initiate fresh acquisition proceedings and has also made a prayer to grant Rs.5.00 lakhs per annum as damages from 1990 to 1999 on the premise that the possession of the land is taken without due process.

sentences.text: The petitioner's aforesaid request was not considered and the petitioner approached this Court in Writ Petition No.80405/2010 with a prayer to quash the acquisition proceeding in so far as the petitioner's land.
The writ was disposed of permitting the petitioner to submit the representation to the State and directing the respondents to consider the representation of the petitioner in accordance with the law.

In the said writ petition, this Court has observed that though the notification is issued under Section 28(4) of the Act, NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 the property survey number is wrongly mentioned as Sy. No.37/1 which is not the petitioner's property, instead of Sy.
No.37/2 the property of the petitioner.
5. After the disposal of Writ Petition No.80405/2010 on 12.07.2011, the petitioner submitted one more representation on 24.09.2011.

The petitioner also filed Writ Appeal No.50435/2012 being aggrieved by non-consideration of his prayer for the refusal to quash the acquisition proceedings in respect of his property bearing Sy. No. 37/2.
The said Writ Appeal was disposed of.
However, liberty was granted to the petitioner to file a representation and all contentions of the petitioner are kept open.
6. After the dismissal of the appeal, the petitioner filed one more representation on 27.08.2012 taking shelter under the observations made in the Writ Appeal.
As the representation remained unanswered, the petitioner filed the present Writ Petition.

7. The petitioner has sought a Writ of Certiorari to quash the notices dated 06.03.1984 and 19.12.1985 at Annexures-B and C issued under Sections 28(1) and 28(4) of the Act, 1966 NC:
2023:KHC-K:1207 respectively and the award at Annexure-D dated 05.08.1998, in so far as it pertains to Sy. No.37/2 of Kapanur village, Taluk and District Kalaburgi.

8. The second prayer, is a writ of mandamus to direct the respondents to issue a fresh notification under Sections 28(1) and 28(4) of the Act of 1966 and to pass a fresh award in respect of Sy. No.37/2 referred to above.

9. The learned counsel for the petitioner during the course of the hearing, on instructions submitted that the petitioner is not pressing the alternative prayer to award compensation under Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1984 at par with the compensation awarded in respect of Sy. No.37/2.
Accordingly, the said alternative prayer is dismissed as not pressed.
10. The respondent KIADB filed a statement of objection.

It is contended that the petition is not maintainable and prayed for dismissal of the petition mainly on the premise that the acquisition proceeding is complete, the award is passed and the amount is deposited and the petitioner can receive the compensation.

It is also contended that the petition is filed long NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 after the acquisition proceedings which were initiated in the year 1984 and by referring to the additional documents submitted on 22.02.2023, it is urged that the project is complete and third-party rights are created and as such the petitioner is not entitled to any relief.
11.

Learned counsel for the petitioner raised the following grounds:
(i) The procedures contemplated under Section 28 of the Act are not followed, notice was not issued under Section 28(2), the enquiry was not held, the award is not notified to the petitioner and compensation is not paid.
(ii) The award starts with the preamble that the award is to be passed in respect of Sy.
No.37/1 measuring 11 acres of Kusnoor village Tq and Dist: Kalaburagi.
However, the operative portion of the award reveals that the award is passed in respect of Sy.37/2 which belongs to the petitioner.

NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 (iii) While issuing notice under Section 28(1), Sy. No.37/2 the property of the petitioner is mentioned, however, in the subsequent notices under Section 28(2) and 28(5) of the Act 1966,
which are not served on the petitioner, Sy. No.37/1 is mentioned.
(iv) Constitutional right under Article 300-A is violated as such the entire proceeding in respect of Sy. No.37/2 is vitiated.

13. Learned counsel for the petitioner in support of her contention submitted that the proceeding gets vitiated and the compensation is to be awarded by issuing a fresh notification under Section 28(1) of the Act and market value is to be determined with reference to the date of fresh Section 28(1) notification.

14. Learned counsel for the respondent, Sri.A.M.Nagaral opposed the petition on the following grounds:
NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 (i) The petition is hit by delay and laches and deserves to be dismissed on the said ground alone as the Section 28(1) notification issued in 1984 sought to be questioned in 2013.

(ii) The land was notified under Section 28(1) in the year 1984 and the notice was sent to the petitioner under Section 28(2) and as the petitioner was not available, the notice was affixed at a conspicuous place and thereafter by following other procedures contemplated, the award is passed and the amount is deposited.
(iii) The documents placed along with the memo dated 22.02.2023 establish that the petitioner is not in possession of the land.

The land has been developed and the third-party rights have been created by allotting the lands to the eligible applicants from 1994 onwards and these facts would establish that the petitioner was aware of the proceedings much earlier than 1994.

15. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent/KIADB would place reliance on the judgment of the Division Bench of this Court in Writ Appeal No.467/2012 in the case of A. Damodar Vs. State of Karnataka and Others - 10 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 supra, wherein this Court has dismissed the writ petition filed three years after the date of knowledge of acquisition proceedings.

sentences.text: 16. This Court considered the contentions raised at the bar and also perused the records and the judgments cited.
17. Admittedly, the petitioner purchased the land bearing Sy. No.37/2 measuring 11 acres under a registered sale deed dated 19.12.1966.
Section 28(1) notification issued on 06.03.1984.

Section 28(1)
notification reveals that Sy. No.37/2 is sought to be acquired along with some other surrounding Spun Pipe And Construction Co.Of India ... vs Spl. Land Acquisition Officer And Ors on 14 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/158833778/

sentences.text:
After issuing Section 28(1) notification to proceed with the acquisition proceedings, notice has to be issued under Section 28(2). Section 28(2) of the Act reads as under:
28: Acquisition of land.-
(1)xxx (2) On publication of a notification under sub- section (1), the State Government shall serve notice upon the owner or where the owner is not the occupier, on the occupier of the land and on all such persons known or believed to be interested therein to show cause, within thirty days from the date of service of the notice, why the land should not be acquired.

During the course of the hearing this Court has directed the respondent - KIADB to produce Section 28(2) notice for having served notice on the owner of the land before proceeding with the acquisition proceeding.
And the matter was adjourned for the said purpose.
However, the said notice is not produced.
19. Learned counsel, Sri.A.M.Nagaral, appearing for KIADB has filed a memo dated 20.03.2023 along with two documents.
The first document is a copy of proceeding and the second document is the letter dated 14.02.1994.

From the copy of the proceedings relating to the acquisition of the land,
it is noticed that reference is made in the said proceeding about the Section 28(2) notice, stating that it was issued to the concerned land owner.
It is stated that notice was served on the land owner by publishing the same in the village panchayat office as the whereabouts of the land owner were not known.

Then, the letter dated 14.02.1994 would also indicate that notices under Section 28(2) and Section 28(6) were issued to the land owner on 10.12.1984 and 31.07.1987, respectively and they are not served on the owner since the owner was not - 12 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 available in the village.
These two documents would demonstrate that notice under Section 28(2) is not personally served on the petitioner.
This is an admission on the part of the respondent-KIADB that notice was not served as the land owner was not available on the land.

20. Answering the contention of the KIADB regarding service of notice by affixure, the learned counsel for the petitioner would submit that the address of the petitioner could have been traced from the registered sale deed pertaining to the property by referring to the mutation entry pertaining to the land and the records from the office of the Sub-Registrar.

The fact that the petitioner has purchased the property under a registered sale deed and the petitioner being a Company has disclosed the address of the registered office of the Company in the sale deed, it was incumbent upon the State/KIADB to issue notice to the registered address shown in the sale deed.

sentences.text: Since such an exercise is not carried out, learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the proceeding is vitiated.

21. On reading Section 28(2), extracted supra, it is apparent that the State Government has to issue notice to the - 13 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 owner and in case the owner is not the occupier of the land, then to the occupier and on all such persons known or believed to be interested therein to show cause within thirty days from the date of service of the notice, why the land should not be acquired.

The expression "State Government shall issue notice" appearing in Section 28(2) leaves no room for any doubt that the notice under Section 28(2) has to be served on the owner of the land, and in case, the owner is not the occupier of the land, then the occupier and all other persons who are interested in the land.
In other words, the notice under Section 28(2) is mandatory.
22. As could be noticed from the language of Section 28(2), it is apparent that Section 28(2) serves an important purpose in the scheme of acquisition.
Section 28(2) is a notice inviting objections, if any, from the owner relating to the proposed land acquisition.
This allows the owner of the land to object to the acquisition proceeding.
The notice contemplated under Section 28(2) is a show-cause-notice.

The right to property being a Constitutional right guaranteed under Article 300-A, any deviation which takes away the opportunity of hearing contemplated under the law violates the constitutional - 14 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 guarantee under Article 300-A.

The learned counsel for the petitioner has relied upon the judgment of the Division Bench of this Court in the case of Abdul Khader Mekhri and Others Vs. The State of Karnataka and Others reported in 1991 (1) KLJ 371 (DB) and also the judgment of the Co-ordinate Bench of this Court in the case of S.C.Kempaiah Vs. KAR Indus.

Area Dev. Board supra.

From the records placed before the Court, it is forthcoming that Section 28(2) notice is not produced.
The inevitable conclusion is Section 28(2) notice is not served on the petitioner.
The petitioner is not heard before passing the award.
Following the ratio laid down in the aforementioned two judgments, no difficulty in holding that the proceeding gets vitiated.

24. Learned counsel for the respondent - KIADB would submit that though Section 28(2) notice did not reflect the correct survey number of the petitioner's land, the same was later amended by initiating a proceeding.
He would refer to the order dated 14.08.1988, wherein this survey number was rectified in respect of an error crept in Section 28(4) notice.

This Court has perused the said proceeding.
The said document would reveal that Sy.No.37 of Kapanur village is having 23 acres and 32 guntas and two sub-divisions i.e., Sy.Nos.37/1, 37/2.
Sy.No.37/1 measures 11 acres, Sy. No.37/2 measures 12 acres and 8 guntas.
This was sought to be rectified by correcting the extent of Sy. No.37/1 as 12 acres 8 guntas and the extent of Sy. No.37/2 as 11 acres 25 guntas.
The document shows that the correction is made after the measurement of land.
However, it is not forthcoming from the record that after this correction, further notice was issued under Section 28(2).
Section 28(4) notice has to be issued after passing the orders under Section 28(3) that too after hearing the objection of the petitioner, if any.
Since notice is not issued to the petitioner under Section 28(2), it is apparent that the Section 28(3) proceeding has not taken place at all.
Under the circumstance, the proceeding said to have been initiated to rectify the survey number and extent of property acquired, belonging to the petitioner, carries no value at all.

For this reason, this Court is of the view that the award which is said to have been passed by the respondent - KIADB in respect of Sy. No.37/2 is not a valid award in the eye of the law and it - 16 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 is already noticed that the award is again not passed in respect of Sy.
No.37/2, it is passed against Sy. No.37/1.
26.
Even the award dated 05.08.1998 which is said to have been passed discloses Sy. No.37/1 as well as Sy. No.37/2.
Though the property acquired is Sy. No.37/2 and in the said award the preamble reveals that the award is being passed in respect of Sy. No.37/1 measuring 11 acres.

Under the circumstance, this Court is of the view that the award said to have been passed by the respondent authority is vitiated and the same is contrary to the mandate of Sections 28(2), 28(3), and 28(4) of the Act.
27. Admittedly, the compensation is not paid to the petitioner.
Notice for having determined the compensation or deposited the compensation is not served on the petitioner.
This is an additional ground to hold that the award is vitiated.

28. However, since learned counsel for respondent No.1, Sri.A.M.Nagaral has urged that the petition must be required to be dismissed on the ground of delay and laches, the said contention is sought to be supported by the view of the Division Bench of this Court in the case of A. Damodar Vs.
- 17 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 State of Karnataka and Others supra, this Court has to consider whether the petition is to be dismissed on the ground of delay and laches though the acquisition proceeding is apparently vitiated for non-compliance of mandatory provisions.
29. This Court has considered the facts in the case of A. Damodar vs. the State of Karnataka referred supra.

30. To this, learned counsel for the petitioner would submit that dispossession is also not made known to the petitioner as the panchanama drawn relating to the delivery of possession refers to Sy.
No.37/1 and not Sy. No.37/2 belonging to the petitioner.

The petitioner contends that it was not aware - 18 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 of the so-called dispossession till the year 2009 and the writ petition is filed in the year 2009, and in the final order passed in the said Writ Petition, the liberty is granted to the petitioner to make a representation.
Thus, it is urged that the cause of action arose only in the year 2009 as such the petition cannot be dismissed on the ground of delay and laches.
31. As already noticed that the petitioner has filed Writ Petition No.80405/2010.
The writ petition was disposed of.
The petitioner has filed a Writ Appeal in W.A.No.50435/2012.
In terms of the order dated 22.08.2012, the Writ Appeal was disposed of.

The relevant observations made in the appeal would read as under:
"The appellant is to furnish a fresh copy of its representation, along with the acknowledgement, to respondent No.1 within a period of one week from today.

Respondent No.1 shall consider and decide the representation in accordance with the law, as expeditiously as possible, and preferably within a period of six weeks from the date of receipt of this order.
4.
All contentions of the appellant, insofar as the representation is concerned are kept open to be - 19 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 raised in appropriate proceedings, if the representation is rejected.
5. With these observations, the appeal is disposed of.
consequently, interim applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
32. The order granting liberty is not questioned by the respondents.
It is required to be noticed that the order granting liberty is the distinguishing factor compared to A. Damodar vs. State of Karnataka case referred supra.

sentences.text: Next question is whether Section 28 (1) notice is to be quashed and the respondents be directed to issue notice afresh under Section 28(1) and be directed to determine and pay the compensation by taking into consideration the date of Section 28(1) notice to be published.
34. To answer this question the court has to find out when the petitioner came to know about his dispossession.
It is the case of the petitioner that he made a representation dated 06.11.2009 marked at Annexure-E to the respondent to cancel Section 28(1) and 28(4) notifications referred to above.

36. However, it is also required to be noticed that the respondent-KIADB has produced certain documents which would disclose the fact that the possession of the land was taken and industrial sites are formed and the sites are allotted to certain persons who had applied for industrial sites in the said area and project is already completed.
The records would also disclose the fact that these developments have taken place from 1994 onwards and have been concluded by the year 2010.

Learned counsel for the respondent -KIADB would urge that all these factors would disclose the fact that the petitioner was aware of the fact that the petitioner was not in possession and also aware of the acquisition proceeding.

In view of the creation of the 3rd party rights in favour of the subsequent allottees, the petitioner at the most is only entitled to compensation and the compensation has to be determined taking the market value of the land that was prevailing in the year 1984 when the notification under Section 28(1) was issued.
It is also the - 21 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 contended by Sri.Nagaral, that Section 28(1) application cannot be quashed as the same has been validly published by following the procedure.
37. Learned counsel for the petitioner would urge that the petitioner was not aware of the acquisition proceeding as there was no notice issued under Section 28(2) of the Act of 1966.

It is also the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that for want of notice under Sections 28(2)
and 28(3), the entire proceeding must be vitiated and no compensation is paid in favour of the petitioner.

There is no notice relating to the award which is said to have been passed by the respondent-State and on account of lapses on the part of the respondent-State, the entire proceeding gets vitiated and there has to be a fresh notification under Section 28(1), given the fact that certain 3rd party rights have been created and the petitioner has to be duly compensated by taking the market value of the land prevailing at the time of 2023 or the market value of the land prevailing at the time of issuance of fresh notification prevailing under Section 28(1) of the Act of 1966.
This Court has considered the contention raised at the bar and also perused the records.

sentences.text: The documents produced by the respondent- KIADB would disclose the fact that the formation of the layout in the land of the petitioner and surrounding lands is complete.

50. Having due regard to the facts of the cases referred to in the judgments referred to above, this Court is of the view that the facts of this case are distinguishable.
In the first place, the petitioner acquiesced to the dispossession.
The petitioner approached the Court 10 years after the dispossession.
However, at the same time in the earlier round of litigation, the petitioner is given the option to make a representation to the respondents to air its grievance.

This being the position, this Court cannot accept the contention of the KIADB that the petitioner is only entitled to compensation determined based on the market value of the land when Section 28(1) notification was issued, in the year 1984 as the procedures under Section 28(2) to 28(5) of the Act of 1966 are not followed.

However, at the same time, the petitioner's claim for determination of compensation based on the present-day valuation also cannot be accepted as the petitioner has acquiesced to the act of KIADB taking possession of the land and has chosen to file the petition in 2009 though the KIADB took possession in 1999.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The expression "State Government shall issue notice" appearing in Section 28(2) leaves no room for any doubt that the notice under Section 28(2) has to be served on the owner of the land, and in case, the owner is not the occupier of the land, then the occupier and all other persons who are interested in the land.
In other words, the notice under Section 28(2) is mandatory.
22. As could be noticed from the language of Section 28(2), it is apparent that Section 28(2) serves an important purpose in the scheme of acquisition.
Section 28(2) is a notice inviting objections, if any, from the owner relating to the proposed land acquisition.
This allows the owner of the land to object to the acquisition proceeding.
The notice contemplated under Section 28(2) is a show-cause-notice.
The right to property being a Constitutional right guaranteed under Article 300-A, any deviation which takes away the opportunity of hearing contemplated under the law violates the constitutional - 14 - NC: 2023:KHC-K:1207 guarantee under Article 300-A.
Since notice is not issued to the petitioner under Section 28(2), it is apparent that the Section 28(3) proceeding has not taken place at all.
